1.pericope_label: After these things Jesus went over the sea of Galilee, which is the sea of Tiberias. And a great multitude followed him, because they saw his miracles which he did on them that were diseased. And Jesus went up into a mountain, and there he sat with his disciples. And the passover, a feast of the Jews, was nigh. When Jesus then lifted up his eyes, and saw a great company come unto him, he saith unto Philip, Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat? And this he said to prove him: for he himself knew what he would do. Philip answered him, Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little. One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, saith unto him, There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many? And Jesus said, Make the men sit down. Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand. And Jesus took the loaves; and when he had given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to them that were set down; and likewise of the fishes as much as they would. When they were filled, he said unto his disciples, Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost. Therefore they gathered them together, and filled twelve baskets with the fragments of the five barley loaves, which remained over and above unto them that had eaten. Then those men, when they had seen the miracle that Jesus did, said, This is of a truth that prophet that should come into the world. When Jesus therefore perceived that they would come and take him by force, to make him a king, he departed again into a mountain himself alone.

schools.summary: Robertson allows a whole year between the previous chapter and this, sees no reason to think the chapters once stood in the other order, and detects in the attempted crowning a movement to start a revolution against Rome. Ellicott refuses both the supposition that part of the Gospel is lost and the attempt to connect the chapters in immediate sequence, since for John the discourse is what the whole is recorded for, and he notes that Matthew and Mark record only that Jesus withdrew to pray, not knowing the reason John supplies. Barnes identifies the prophet of the acclamation as the Messiah and traces the crowd's error to their supposing him a temporal prince. Lightfoot sets the loaves beside Elisha's feeding, where the rabbis enlarge the number fed to two thousand two hundred.

Calvin explains why the miracle appears here at all, against John's custom of supplying what the others omit: he repeats it expressly in order to pass from it to the sermon at Capernaum. On the thanksgiving he draws the rule that whenever we take food we ought to begin with prayer, and on the attempted crowning he allows some ground for the title of king while putting the error in their taking on themselves the liberty of appointing one. Gill leaves open whether the lad belonged to Christ and the disciples, which would show how meanly they lived, or came to sell, and says Christ perceived their purpose as the God who knows the heart.

Clarke supplies the economics of the loaves, barley bearing scarcely a third of the value of wheat, and cites the handfuls of barley for which false prophetesses polluted the name of God as the measure of so mean a fare. Wesley says ten or eleven months of history must be supplied from the other evangelists, and guesses that Philip had the care of providing victuals for the apostles.
Henry gives the motive of the crowd plainly, their hearts being set on making him a king, and calls the attempt irregular zeal in Christ's followers.

Chrysostom takes the retirement for a lesson in method: missiles rebound with great force from a hard body where a softer material stops them, so violent men are only excited by violence and softened by gentleness, and Christ quieted the irritation of the Jews by withdrawing from Jerusalem.
Bede puts the motive of the would-be kingmakers most simply, that men like a merciful king to rule over them and a powerful one to protect them.

debates.question: Why did Jesus withdraw to the mountain alone?

positions.position: To avoid a crowd that would have made him a temporal king and borne him to the royal city
Because they usurped a prerogative belonging to God alone in appointing a king
Because gentleness disarms violent men where resistance inflames them

outliers.claim: Brings in the rabbinic estimate of the passover throng, King Agrippa counting the paschal lambs by having one kidney of each laid aside

16.pericope_label: And when even was now come, his disciples went down unto the sea, And entered into a ship, and went over the sea toward Capernaum. And it was now dark, and Jesus was not come to them. And the sea arose by reason of a great wind that blew. So when they had rowed about five and twenty or thirty furlongs, they see Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing nigh unto the ship: and they were afraid. But he saith unto them, It is I; be not afraid. Then they willingly received him into the ship: and immediately the ship was at the land whither they went.

schools.summary: Robertson distinguishes this late evening, the real one, from the mid-afternoon evening of the earlier narrative, reads the tenses as dramatic writing with two past perfects against an imperfect, makes the distance a little over halfway across a lake of some six miles, and calls the last verb inchoative, that they began to be willing. Ellicott notes that the better text has not a ship but the ship in which they first crossed, that the verb means they were going over with the voyage still continuing, and that the Greek says no more than that they were willing to receive him, though Matthew and Mark state that they did. Barnes denies there is any evidence of a miracle in the landing, since we do not know how far from land they were and the word rendered immediately means only that no long interval passed.

Calvin supplies the reason for the separation, that Christ meant to conceal himself until the crowd dispersed, since a popular tumult is not easily allayed and a stain once fixed would not easily be wiped off; he remarks how much John passes over that the others tell, explains the terror from their taking him for an apparition, and insists that it is in Christ's presence alone that we have grounds of confidence, though this belongs exclusively to his disciples. Gill divides the evenings, the first having fallen before they sat down to eat, and has the disciples receive him the more gladly for being in distress.

Clarke observes that Mark has them ordered to Bethsaida while in the event they landed in Gennesaret, supposes the two towns lay a few miles apart on the same shore, notes that the vessel was small and no sail could be carried in such a wind, and thinks the evangelist speaks of the sudden arrival as extraordinary and miraculous.
Chrysostom draws the pastoral point from the separation, that Christ provides for the good of his disciples not only when present in the body but also when far away.

positions.position: Yes: the evangelist speaks of the sudden arrival as extraordinary
No: the word rendered immediately means only that no long interval passed

outliers.claim: Finds in the disciples' terror at the figure on the water a mirror of what knowledge of Christ men can reach without his word

22.pericope_label: The day following, when the people which stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was none other boat there, save that one whereinto his disciples were entered, and that Jesus went not with his disciples into the boat, but that his disciples were gone away alone; (Howbeit there came other boats from Tiberias nigh unto the place where they did eat bread, after that the Lord had given thanks:) When the people therefore saw that Jesus was not there, neither his disciples, they also took shipping, and came to Capernaum, seeking for Jesus. And when they had found him on the other side of the sea, they said unto him, Rabbi, when camest thou hither? Jesus answered them and said, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Ye seek me, not because ye saw the miracles, but because ye did eat of the loaves, and were filled. Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life, which the Son of man shall give unto you: for him hath God the Father sealed.

schools.summary: Barnes explains the phrase about the other side from the standpoint of a writer living on the west, allows that to seek Christ because the miracles proved him sent from God would have been proper, and calls following him merely because their wants were supplied a gross selfishness, adding that many still seek religion from no better motive; on the command he denies that it forbids effort for the supply of our wants, only anxiety and the making of this the supreme object. Ellicott points out that the starting point of the narrative shifts within a few verses, puts the meeting in the synagogue at Capernaum, says there is an earlier sign than the one they ask about whose meaning neither they nor the disciples have grasped, and prefers the marginal work not to labour not, since it preserves the connection with the questions that follow. Robertson takes the present imperative as a prohibition of the habit and reads the perishing meat against a crowd already hungry again. Lightfoot closes with the rabbis on the seal of God, which one of them names Truth.

Calvin sets the crowd's inference out as a chain, that there had been only one boat, that they saw it leave without him, that other boats came next day, and that they found him at Capernaum, so he must have crossed miraculously; he adds the geography that makes the shores confusing, chides them for pressing forward without considering why they had come, and explains the shape of the command, that because our understandings are gross the disease is corrected first and the duty pointed out after. Gill notes that Christ could have told them how he came and would not gratify the curiosity.

Clarke denies the crowd were in Perea at all, citing Bishop Pearce that the Greek word can mean on the side of as well as beyond, and complains that though the miracle was among the most astonishing ever wrought, and attested by all their senses, many regarded the hand of God in it no further than it satisfied their appetite. Wesley explains why any were still there, held by the want of vessels and staying the less unwillingly for seeing that Jesus had not embarked, and says Christ begins here to try their sincerity, having until now been gathering hearers.
Henry gives the motive of the search plainly, their hearts being set on making him a king, so that they lay in wait for his return.

Chrysostom makes the inference the point of the paragraph, that Christ did not show himself walking on the sea but gave them the means of inferring it, and defends the sharpness of the rebuke, since the mild and gentle is not always useful and a dull hearer must be roused with a goad.

debates.question: Where were the people standing when they saw the boats?

positions.position: On the eastern shore, the writer's phrase being relative to his own position in the west
Not in Perea at all: the Greek word can mean on the side of as well as beyond

outliers.claim: Prefers the margin to the text, since work not rather than labour not keeps the verbal link with the questions that follow

28.pericope_label: Then said they unto him, What shall we do, that we might work the works of God? Jesus answered and said unto them, This is the work of God, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent. They said therefore unto him, What sign shewest thou then, that we may see, and believe thee? what dost thou work? Our fathers did eat manna in the desert; as it is written, He gave them bread from heaven to eat. Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Moses gave you not that bread from heaven; but my Father giveth you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he which cometh down from heaven, and giveth life unto the world. Then said they unto him, Lord, evermore give us this bread.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the question confirms the sense given to the command before it, since they grasp that there are works appointed of God, puts the logic of their challenge as the Messiah being greater than Moses while the sign shown was less, and hears in their final request the same mistake as the Samaritan woman's, preferring to render the address Sir rather than Lord. Robertson makes the question a deliberative subjunctive, what are we to do as a habit, observes that Jesus calls belief in himself the work of God where these hearers thought of Pharisaic deeds, reports that the rabbis proved from a psalm that the Messiah would outdo Moses with bread from heaven, and calls the reply a blunt and pointed denial that Moses was the giver at all. Barnes is careful that the answer is not quietism, since Jesus did not tell them they had nothing to do but that a work remained and was imperative. Lightfoot says the nation looked for the dainties their Messiah was to bring, manna above all.

Calvin agrees they understood they were called higher than the conveniences of the present life and puts the mistake elsewhere; he adds that all men undertake without faith is vain, explains how the denial about Moses stands beside the psalm by taking it as a comparison, the manna nourishing the body where the true bread gives life to the soul, and takes their closing request for irony, an accusation of vain boasting. Gill locates the error of the first question exactly, that they imagined eternal life was to be obtained by working.

Clarke puts their argument in their own mouths, that five thousand fed once is little beside a million fed for forty years, sets the refutation out in four steps, and leaves both doors open on the closing request, either that the manna be renewed or that the bread just spoken of become their constant nourishment. Wesley distinguishes two heavens, the lower sublunary one from which the manna fell and the highest, from which, as he counts, Jesus says seven times in this discourse that he came down, and reads the closing request as still literal yet not far from believing.
Henry notices the manner rather than the matter: Christ gave them leave to ask and did not resent the interruption as an affront.

debates.question: What do they mean by asking for this bread evermore?

positions.position: Irony, an accusation of vain boasting
A literal request, yet from men not far from believing
The same misunderstanding as the Samaritan woman's, a thought of physical need

debates.question: What makes the work of God one work rather than many?

positions.position: That separate acts are the outcome of a principle, where they thought of life as an aggregate of deeds
That belief in Christ is itself the work God requires, against the Pharisaic deeds they had in mind

outliers.claim: Counts seven places in the discourse where Jesus says he came down from heaven, and distinguishes that heaven from the sublunary one the manna fell from

35.pericope_label: And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst. But I said unto you, That ye also have seen me, and believe not. All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me. And this is the Father’s will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day. And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.

schools.summary: Robertson calls the great sentence startling in the extreme and guards it from a false parallel, since Philo compares the manna to the divine Word only allegorically and vaguely; he notes the collective neuter singular in the saying about those the Father gives, marks the perfect tense of the coming down, and makes the closing subjunctive continuous, that the believer may keep on having eternal life. Ellicott hears the answer to their own request, since they had asked for this bread and it now stands present before them, observes that Christ identifies his own will with the Father's while still asserting that he has one of his own, and prefers the best manuscripts in the closing verses, which keep the relation of Father and Son in view. Barnes takes the point of the sender's will to be faithfulness to a trust, says Christ never left a doctrine so stated without guarding it, and that seeing was not enough, many Jews having seen him and few believed. Lightfoot supplies the background of the phrase about the last day, the nation looking for the resurrection at the Messiah's coming.

Calvin says what they demanded in mockery is set before their eyes, and that the doctrine has two parts, whence life is to be sought and how enjoyed; he takes the obstinacy of these hearers as proof that they are reprobate and no part of the flock, infers that all who do not profit by the Gospel willingly draw ruin on themselves, and reduces the last verse to a rule, that the way to salvation is to obey the Gospel. Gill limits the term of those given from both sides, that it means neither the apostles only nor every individual of mankind.

Clarke takes the neuter for the masculine and adds the qualification that governs his whole reading, that those drawn are led and not driven, since as many as are led by the Spirit of God are the children of God; on losing nothing he distinguishes that God may will a thing to be without willing that it shall be, and wills perseverance without forcing it, Judas having been given to Christ and lost; and he makes explicit that so far from any being excluded it is God's will that every one who sees may believe. Wesley describes the given as those who feel themselves lost and follow the drawings of the Father, promises them pardon, holiness and heaven if they endure to the end, and says the promise holds if they endure, as Judas did not.
Chrysostom marks where the discourse turns, since Christ now begins to set forth mysteries and speaks first of his divinity, not of his body, which comes only at the end.

debates.question: Why do some come to Christ and others not?

positions.position: Because the obstinate are reprobate and no part of the flock, the distinction keeping the doctrine's authority unimpaired
Because those drawn are led and not driven, God willing perseverance without forcing it

outliers.claim: Rules out the Philo parallel, since his comparison of manna to the divine Word is allegorical and vague where this language is not

41.pericope_label: The Jews then murmured at him, because he said, I am the bread which came down from heaven. And they said, Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven? Jesus therefore answered and said unto them, Murmur not among yourselves. No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day. It is written in the prophets, And they shall be all taught of God. Every man therefore that hath heard, and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto me. Not that any man hath seen the Father, save he which is of God, he hath seen the Father. Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life. I am that bread of life. Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead. This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.

schools.summary: Robertson notes that the verb for murmuring is onomatopoetic, used in the Greek Old Testament of murmuring against Moses, and likens it to the cooing of doves or the buzzing of bees; on the drawing he observes that the verb can mean to drag, as of a net or a sword, but that here it is a drawing by moral power, and that since no one has seen God with the eyes the only way to see him is to see Christ. Ellicott would render the first verb murmured concerning him and finds the true spirit of objectors in it, fastening on whatever they do not understand in its most startling form; he makes the relation of hearing and seeing exact, that hearing the Father was preparation for the fuller revelation in the Son and not a substitute for it, and marks the change from bread that is of life to bread that is living, containing the principle of life in itself. Barnes takes the prophets for the book of the prophets, and says the guard about no man having seen the Father was added because a pupil commonly sees his teacher where this teaching is of another kind. Lightfoot hears in the last clause a quiet refutation of the expected Messianic dainties, since all the dainties Christ provided were himself.

Calvin locates the offence in the meanness of Christ's human condition, in which they perceived nothing divine, takes the saying about drawing as reminding them that to embrace this doctrine is a peculiar gift, explains the plural prophets by the collection of all the prophecies into one volume, insists that both halves be joined, since no knowledge of Christ can be had until the Father enlightens the naturally blind and yet it is vain to seek God apart from Christ, and explains the repetition itself, that nothing is more necessary to be known and every man feels how hard it is to believe. Gill puts the inability flatly, that men in an unregenerate state have neither the power nor the will.

Clarke finds the drift of the discourse the real cause of the murmuring, since it went to prove him greater than Moses, and answers the hard saying about drawing with the poet's line quoted by Augustine, that every man is drawn by his own delight: show green herbage to a sheep and he is drawn, show nuts to a child and he is drawn; he adds that God teaches by his Spirit and not in person. Wesley states the same as a balance, that no man can believe unless God give him power and God draws first by good desires, not by compulsion nor by laying the will under necessity, and enters the caution that marks his school, that the whole discourse refers directly to the passion and only remotely, if at all, to the Supper.

Chrysostom traces the timing of the complaint, that while they hoped for food they could eat they had no misgivings, and it began only when that hope was taken away, so the reason they gave was a pretence.
Augustine states the double reference: Christ calls himself bread not only in respect of the divinity which feeds all things but of the human nature assumed by the Word.

debates.question: How is the Father's drawing to be understood?

positions.position: As a drawing by moral power, not a dragging
As delight: every man is drawn by what he loves, as a sheep by herbage or a child by nuts
As a peculiar gift of God, named so that the unbelief of many should not disturb weaker minds
As power given without compulsion, God drawing first by good desires

outliers.claim: Holds that the whole discourse on flesh and blood refers directly to the passion and only remotely, if at all, to the Lord's Supper

52.pericope_label: The Jews therefore strove among themselves, saying, How can this man give us his flesh to eat? Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you. Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day. For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed. He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him. As the living Father hath sent me, and I live by the Father: so he that eateth me, even he shall live by me. This is that bread which came down from heaven: not as your fathers did eat manna, and are dead: he that eateth of this bread shall live for ever. These things said he in the synagogue, as he taught in Capernaum.

schools.summary: Robertson notes the verb for striving is used of armed combat before a war of words and calls the imperfect inchoative, the murmuring having now become bitter contention; he prefers the adjective to the adverb on the best manuscripts, so the sense is true food and true drink, says the verb for abiding expresses a continual mystical fellowship, and calls the closing verse a final explanation of the true manna. Ellicott marks the advance, that they now understand him to mean his flesh is to be eaten though his words have not yet said so, renders the same verse true food, prefers abideth to dwelleth and calls it one of those deeper thoughts which meet us only in the beloved disciple, and notes that the tense at the close has moved into the past. Barnes denies flatly that the command can be literal, the thing never having been done and nothing being more absurd than to suppose it intended.

Calvin says the name Jews is used not by way of honour but to reproach an unbelief that will not even inquire modestly, hears in the oath a just resentment at grace rejected with disdain, supplies the comparison that makes the saying intelligible, that as the body is consumed for want of food so the soul perishes if not fed with heavenly bread, adds that there is no other way for Christ to become ours than by faith directed to his flesh, and ends on the count, that out of so great a multitude scarcely a few profited. Gill notes that the difficulty is not removed until the discourse ends, and that all this was said openly in the place of public worship.

Clarke gives the sense of eating as being made partakers of the blessings purchased by the passion, keeping the analogy running, finds a deliberate figure in the indwelling, since of all unions none is so intimate as that effected by digesting food, and observes that the interruptions throughout only gave fuller opportunity to proclaim the whole truth about the passion. Wesley notes the ascending order of the chapter, the Jews tried here, the disciples next, the apostles last, and puts the sense in a line, that eating his flesh is another expression for believing.
Henry glosses flesh and blood together as the Redeemer in the nature of man, Christ crucified and the redemption wrought by him.

Augustine turns the striving into a contrast, that the Jews strove because they did not understand what the bread of peace was, where those who eat that bread do not strive, God making them dwell together in unity. Bede sets out what the change of wording is for, to show the difference between bodily meat and drink and the spiritual mystery of the body and blood.

debates.question: How is the eating of the flesh to be taken?

positions.position: Not literally at all, the supposition being absurd
As being made partakers of the blessings purchased by the passion
As another expression for believing
As faith directed to his flesh, which is the only way Christ becomes ours

outliers.claim: Reads the mutual indwelling from the physiology of eating, since food is changed into the substance of the one who eats it, and takes that for the model our Lord chose

60.pericope_label: Many therefore of his disciples, when they had heard this, said, This is an hard saying; who can hear it? When Jesus knew in himself that his disciples murmured at it, he said unto them, Doth this offend you? What and if ye shall see the Son of man ascend up where he was before? It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life. But there are some of you that believe not. For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were that believed not, and who should betray him. And he said, Therefore said I unto you, that no man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father.

schools.summary: Robertson glosses the adjective in the complaint as rough, harsh, dried hard, takes the hard saying to be the last one about eating him, marks the articular participle in the saying about the Spirit, and notes that the closing verse makes the same point as the earlier one about drawing with a different verb. Ellicott agrees that disciple is used here in the wider sense though he thinks the apostles not excluded, notes that the tenses put the scene in the present with the knowing and the murmuring together, agrees that the ascension would be the proof of the coming down, and gives the figure of the unprepared fields, where it is vain to sow and the defection proves the hearts unready without touching the goodness of the seed. Barnes is careful that disciple means learner and does not of itself imply a real Christian, and denies that the word spirit here means the Holy Ghost, since the next clause makes the words themselves spirit.

Calvin puts the hardness in their hearts and not in the word, since the reprobate make stones of God's word to dash themselves upon; he finds in the question about the ascension a lifting of the veil, says the spiritual character of the doctrine explains why the hearers did not profit, holds that they corrupted a quickening doctrine for want of faith, and takes the last verse as a caution against astonishment that the Gospel is not everywhere received. Gill takes the preceding verse for proof of divinity, since Christ knew their murmuring in himself without being told.

Clarke renders the objection as a question about digesting such doctrine, which they found intolerable, recalls a similar phrase in Euripides, takes the ascension as removing the offence since they would soon have full proof that the saying was figurative, says it is the spiritual sense only that is to be attended to, and applies the warning about unbelief to Judas and those who afterwards left. Wesley turns the complaint around, hard to the children of the world and sweet to the children of God, asks how much more incredible the giving of his flesh would then appear, makes the flesh the bare carnal literal meaning which profits nothing, and draws the line that God foresees future contingencies while his foreknowledge is not their cause.
Henry sums the effect: the discourse was to some a savour of death unto death, not to the Jews only but to disciples.
Augustine describes the misunderstanding exactly: taking the words in a human sense, they supposed he spoke of cutting up the flesh of the Word for distribution.

debates.question: Does the question about the ascension lessen the offence or increase it?

positions.position: Lessens it, since seeing him ascend would prove the saying figurative
Increases it, a further doctrine quite as offensive being stated instead of an explanation
Neither: it withdraws the veil of his mean condition and calls them to behold a heavenly glory

outliers.claim: States the foreknowledge carefully, that God foresees future contingencies while his foreknowledge is not their cause

themes: Many therefore of his disciples, when they had heard this, said, This is an hard saying; who can hear it?
When Jesus knew in himself that his disciples murmured at it, he said unto them, Doth this offend you?
What and if ye shall see the Son of man ascend up where he was before?
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
But there are some of you that believe not. For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were that believed not, and who should betray him.
And he said, Therefore said I unto you, that no man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father.

66.pericope_label: From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away? Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life. And we believe and are sure that thou art that Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus answered them, Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil? He spake of Judas Iscariot the son of Simon: for he it was that should betray him, being one of the twelve.

schools.summary: Robertson says Jesus drew the line of cleavage between true and false believers, notes the Greek of the question to the twelve expects the answer no, wonders whether Judas showed some sympathy with the departing crowds while keeping still, and renders the confession as perfects, we have come to believe and still believe. Ellicott corrects the English of the opening, since the Greek has no word for time and probably means on that account, suggests the look may have been directed to Peter, finds the speech striking since they had left all to follow and found all in him, says the faith which first burned in their hearts has passed into the calm certainty of settled knowledge, and sees the brightness of that hope crossed by a shadow. Barnes limits who went back, draws the lesson that we need not wonder at the apostasy of many who profess to follow Christ, calls Peter's answer characteristic, notes that he says we in the name of the whole company while one among them had no such feeling, and hears the emphasis in the pronoun of the last verse, that it is the greater sin to betray one who chose them in love.

Calvin calls the desertion a consequence of the sermon, gives the pastoral reason for the question to the twelve, that the faith of the apostles might well be shaken at finding themselves so small a remnant, says Peter's reply has two clauses and that all were of the same mind except that in Judas there was no sincerity, thinks Christ was fortifying the eleven against an offence already at hand, and observes that Judas is not recorded to have been moved at all. Gill limits the departure to the wider body of disciples, not the twelve and not the seventy, and dates the apostles' faith from the first call.

Clarke says the departing no longer acknowledged him as Messiah and that none of them were of the twelve, makes the question to the twelve emphatic, will you abandon me whom I have distinguished with innumerable marks of affection, calls Peter's answer his usual zeal and readiness, and glosses the word for devil as an accuser enlisted on Satan's side. Wesley says our Lord now began to purge his floor, the proud and careless driven away and those remaining who were fit for the Master's use, reduces Peter's first clause to its point, that Christ alone speaks the words which show the way to life everlasting, and reads the last verse as a gracious warning on which Judas ought to have repented, inferring that men may fall even from such an election.
Henry draws the warning, that when we admit hard thoughts of the words and works of Jesus we enter into a temptation which, unless mercy prevent, ends in drawing back.

debates.question: What does the naming of a devil among the twelve imply?

positions.position: That Judas is one now, not that he was one when chosen
That men may fall even from such an election, the warning being gracious
That Christ was fortifying the eleven beforehand against an offence already at hand

outliers.claim: Observes that Judas, for all his bad conscience, is not recorded to have been moved by the warning at all

themes: From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.
